blocks.Intent: Holds the desired state and what must stay true. Here: intent.md, the requirements and the candidate file, all in Git.
blocks.Collector: Reads the live network. Here: Forward's headless collector, over SSH, collection mode only.
blocks.Observability: Keeps the network's actual state and flags what differs from intent. Here: Forward's model and Predict, judged by the requirements.
blocks.Orchestrator: Sequences the other blocks on events and never touches a device. Here: the pull request and its forward/predict check.
blocks.Executor: Makes the change on the network. Here: NAPALM, sending the exact bytes Predict judged.
blocks.Network: The thing being managed. Here: four cEOS routers, a client and a service, built by netlab and containerlab.

lab.title: Start your lab
lab.what: Nothing starts until you press the button. netlab reads lab/topology.yml (four routers, a client and a service, and their links) and has containerlab start them, without configuring them. Then NAPALM writes each router's baseline configuration over eAPI, so there is exactly one way a change gets onto a router. You can watch the lab in the Containerlab panel in the left bar of VS Code: open a terminal on any router or on the client and the service.

before.q: netlab builds the topology. What puts the baseline configuration on the routers?
before.why: NAPALM. Every change in this workshop, baseline, candidate and restore, takes the same path, which is what lets Deploy check it. The collector only reads.

before.q: netlab starts your lab with --no-config. What does that mean?
options: It builds and links the nodes but leaves them unconfigured
before.why: netlab only defines and launches the topology. The configuration comes from the baseline files through NAPALM, which keeps one change path for the whole workshop.

after.q: How many containers should be running?
options: 6: four routers, a client and a service
after.why: Six. The client and the service are what the requirements test from: can the client still reach the service?

run.label: Start the lab
run.note: Takes 2 to 3 minutes. You will see netlab start the six nodes, then the baseline go on. The machine will be busy; that is normal.

run.label: Check my setup
run.note: Checks tools, your Forward access and the lab.

lab.catchup: Starts the lab if it isn't running and applies the baseline configuration. Nothing else changes.

baseline.title: Give Forward a baseline
baseline.what: The headless collector logs in to each router, reads its configuration and state, and writes a snapshot. Forward turns it into a model of your network and checks the baseline requirements on it. That model is the known-good starting point every later prediction is compared with.

before.q: What does a baseline give you that logging in and running show commands doesn't?
options: Nothing, it is the same information
A saved, queryable model to compare a prediction against
A backup of the router configs
before.why: A frozen model of what is true now. Without it, a prediction has nothing to be 'different from'.

after.q: The baseline requirements did not all PASS. Should you carry on?
options: Yes, the change might fix them
Yes, but only to the next step
after.why: Stop. Predicting from a broken start tells you nothing about your change. The gate treats it the same way.

run.label: Collect the baseline
run.note: Reads all four routers and uploads the snapshot. About a minute.

baseline.catchup: Makes sure the lab is up, puts r4's advertisements back to the baseline and takes a fresh baseline.

data.title: What Forward found: your devices
data.why: Forward read these straight from the routers. This is the inventory it builds everything else on.

data.title: Who can reach the service prefix
data.why: Every device's route to 10.20.20.0/24, from Forward's model of the baseline.

data.title: What Forward knows about this software
data.why: Published CVEs for this OS, from Forward's CVE index. The same data exists for a real network.

change.title: Write the change
change.what: r4 advertises three prefixes into BGP. Two are stale leftovers; one carries the live service. You describe the change as lines in a file under version control. That file is the desired state, and nothing reaches a router until later steps approve it.

before.q: The service is at 10.20.20.20. Which of r4's three advertisements carries it?
before.why: 10.20.20.0/24 contains 10.20.20.20. The other two are the stale ones. They look identical in the configuration, which is the whole problem.

after.q: Say you retire 10.20.20.0/24. Which router shows the damage?
options: r4, where you made the change
r1, two hops away, which loses its route
after.why: r1 loses its only route to the service. The change is on r4; the damage is not. That distance is why review of the diff misses it.

change.catchup: Makes sure the lab is up, puts r4's advertisements back to the baseline and takes a fresh baseline. It also clears your candidate, so you start the change from nothing.

predict.title: Predict it
predict.what: Predict applies your candidate lines to Forward's model of the baseline and builds the network that would result. Every requirement is evaluated on that predicted network. No router is touched. The verdict, the candidate hash and the baseline id are written to evidence.json.

before.q: Does predicting send anything to your routers?
options: No: it only changes the model
Only the lines that are safe
before.why: Nothing is sent. That is what makes it safe to try a change you suspect is bad.

after.q: A requirement FAILed. What does that tell you?
options: The change would break something the requirements protect
after.why: FAIL means the predicted network violates a requirement. A syntax error is caught earlier, and a Forward error shows as ERROR, which also blocks.

run.label: Predict my change
run.note: Runs the same check as the pull request, locally. A minute or two.

predict.catchup: Makes sure the lab is up, puts r4's advertisements back to the baseline and takes a fresh baseline. It writes the known-good change (retire the two stale prefixes) so you can carry on from here. You still predict, approve, deploy and verify it yourself. Your candidate file is replaced.

data.title: What your change does to the routing tables
data.why: Forward compared the baseline model with the predicted one. These are the routes that would change.

approve.title: Review and approve
approve.what: Opening a pull request is the event that makes the pipeline run: it triggers the forward/predict check. The pipeline never writes to a router. Merging a green check is the human approval, and it is bound to this exact change.

before.q: Who decides the change is safe to deploy?
options: The tests, plus a person who read the result
before.why: The requirements decide; a person approves. Forward AI explains and advises, but it never decides.

after.q: What is your approval tied to?
options: The candidate hash, the baseline and the requirements together
after.why: Change any of the three and deploy refuses, so you cannot approve one change and ship another.

approve.catchup: Makes sure the lab is up, puts r4's advertisements back to the baseline and takes a fresh baseline. It writes the known-good change as the candidate. You still open the pull request and approve it yourself. Your candidate file is replaced.

data.title: What you are approving, as routing changes
data.why: The same comparison: read it before you merge.

deploy.title: Deploy exactly what was predicted
deploy.what: NAPALM sends the very same lines Predict judged to r4. Before it writes, deploy checks that the PR is merged and green, that the baseline is still current, that no router has drifted since, and that nobody else holds the lab's lock. The router then computes the diff for the change, and deploy prints it before committing. You confirm by typing the start of the candidate's hash.

before.q: Why must you type the first 7 characters of the hash yourself?
options: To prove you reviewed this exact change, not a different one
before.why: A button can be clicked without reading. The hash on screen is the one Predict judged; typing it ties your approval to those bytes.

after.q: Someone edits a router by hand after your baseline. What does deploy do?
options: Refuses: the live network drifted from what was predicted
after.why: It refuses. The prediction was about a network that no longer exists, which is the STALE outcome.

deploy.catchup: Makes sure the lab is up, puts r4's advertisements back to the baseline and takes a fresh baseline. Use this if Deploy keeps saying STALE or the routers drifted. This restarts the loop from the Change step: your merged change stays on main, and the new baseline makes the old approval stale. Make your next change on a new branch. Your candidate file is cleared.

data.title: What you are about to ship, as routing changes
data.why: Predicted, not yet real: deploy sends exactly the change that produced this.

verify.title: Verify on the real network
verify.what: Now the same two blocks run again, on the real network. The collector reads it, Forward evaluates every requirement, and the result is compared line by line with what Predict said. Probes also test the real flows from the client.

options: Reality matches the prediction on every requirement
The change was a good idea
before.why: MATCH is about the model being right. Whether the change was good is what the requirements already said.

after.q: It says MISMATCH. What does that tell you?
options: The model and the network disagree: investigate, and restore if it matters
Run verify again until it matches
after.why: The prediction and reality diverge, which is the case the whole method exists to surface. Never retry until green.

run.label: Verify the network
run.note: Probes the real flows, collects again and compares.

run.label: Just test the flows
run.note: TCP 8080 should work, TCP 2222 must be refused.

verify.catchup: Makes sure the lab is up, puts r4's advertisements back to the baseline and takes a fresh baseline. This restarts the loop from the Change step: your merged change stays on main, and the new baseline makes the old approval stale. Make your next change on a new branch. Your candidate file is cleared.

data.title: What really changed in the network
data.why: Baseline against the network collected after deploy: the real routing changes.

done.title: Loop closed
done.what: You predicted, approved, deployed and verified. To go again, restore r4's baseline advertisements (NAPALM, the same path as everything else) and take a fresh baseline.

before.q: Why take a new baseline after a restore?
options: The network changed, so the old model is stale
before.why: Predictions compare with the baseline. After a restore it describes a network that no longer exists.

done.catchup: Makes sure the lab is up, puts r4's advertisements back to the baseline and takes a fresh baseline. It clears your candidate, ready for another go.

terms.BGP: Border Gateway Protocol: how these routers tell each other which networks they can reach.
terms.prefix: A block of IP addresses written like 10.20.20.0/24.
terms.advertisement: A router telling its neighbors "I can reach this prefix". r4 advertises three.
terms.advertisements: A router telling its neighbors "I can reach this prefix". r4 advertises three.
terms.stale: Left over and no longer needed, but still announced.
terms.ACL: Access control list: the rule list on r1 that decides which traffic is allowed through.
terms.NQE: Network Query Engine: Forward's way of asking a question of the whole network model.
terms.snapshot: A saved picture of the network's configuration and state at one moment.
terms.baseline: The snapshot taken before the change: what is true now, and the starting point for every comparison.
terms.requirement: A statement about what must be true, such as "the client can reach the service on 8080". Requirements decide the verdict.
terms.requirements: Statements about what must be true, such as "the client can reach the service on 8080". They decide the verdict.
terms.prediction: Forward's model of the network after your change, built without touching any router.
terms.Predict: The Forward feature that builds that model and checks the requirements on it.
terms.candidate: The file holding your proposed change.
terms.eAPI: Arista's HTTPS interface for configuring and reading a router.
terms.netlab: The tool that describes the lab (routers, links, addresses) and has containerlab start it.
terms.containerlab: The tool that runs network devices as containers.
terms.drift: The network no longer matching what was predicted, for example because someone edited a router by hand.
terms.hash: A short fingerprint of a file. If one character of the change differs, the hash differs.
terms.collector: Forward's tool that logs in to the devices and reads their configuration and state.

lane.title: Explore what Forward knows
lane.why: Devices, routes, CVEs and routing changes, straight from Forward's model, with filters. Read the sentence first; open the raw JSON to see exactly what Forward returned.

lane.title: Write your own requirement
lane.why: r1's ACL blocks HTTPS (TCP 8443) too, but no requirement says it must stay blocked. Add one and see the prediction judge it.

lane.title: Predict every way of retiring r4's statements
lane.why: Four changes, predicted side by side: which pass, which fail, and why. No router is touched.
lane.label: Run the comparison
lane.note: Takes several minutes: it runs one prediction per change.

lane_ai.title: Ask Forward AI about your network
lane_ai.why: A chat grounded in one snapshot. It explains; the requirements still decide.

lane_ai.title: Have a prediction explained
lane_ai.why: Forward AI summarizes what the change alters and what it affects.
lane_ai.label: Explain my prediction

lane_ai.title: Let Forward AI draft the change
lane_ai.why: Shows a draft from intent.md. It is checked against the same scope rules and predicted like any other change.
lane_ai.label: Show a draft

lane_ai.title: Let an agent iterate to a passing change
lane_ai.why: Draft, predict, adjust, repeat, stopping before approval. Compare its answer with yours.
lane_ai.label: Run the agent
lane_ai.note: Takes several minutes. It replaces your candidate file.
